title: Colossians
subtitle: All the fullness of God, in one who lived in a body
lead: Colossians is a short letter to a small church in the Lycus valley of Phrygia, in what is now western Turkey. The church had been founded not by Paul but by a local man, Epaphras, and some of its members were being drawn to a teaching that promised more: visions, rules about food and holy days, fasting, and some kind of devotion to angels. The letter answers with Christ. In him 'all the fullness of deity makes its home bodily' (2:9), every power in heaven was created in him and was defeated at his cross, and believers already have everything in him.

At the center of the letter stands one of the highest passages about Christ in the New Testament, the hymn of 1:15-20: 'He is the image of the God who cannot be seen, the firstborn of all creation.' The letter then draws a practical line from the throne of God to the kitchen table: since you were raised with Christ, take off the old self, put on love, and live in your households, as wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters, under one Lord. It closes with greetings from Paul's companions, among them Mark, Luke and Onesimus, the slave of Philemon's household whose story the letter to Philemon tells.
facts: Traditionally Paul, with Timothy named as co-sender (1:1; 4:18). Many scholars hold that a coworker or a later follower wrote it in Paul's name. See the authorship table.

If Paul wrote it: on the traditional view from Rome during his first imprisonment, about AD 62; others suggest Caesarea or Ephesus, earlier. If a follower wrote it: dates from about AD 70 (Gnilka) or 80 (Lohse) to as late as about AD 90 have been proposed.
Paul is a prisoner (4:3, 10, 18); the place is not named. The Textus Receptus adds a later note, 'written from Rome'.
The church at Colossae, mostly Gentile, founded by Epaphras; the letter is also to be read in Laodicea (4:16).
A letter: greeting, thanksgiving and prayer, a hymn about Christ, a warning against a rival teaching, instruction for life, a household code, greetings.
Ephesians (much shared wording) and Philemon (the same people, probably sent together)
authorship: It opens 'Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus ... and Timothy our brother' (1:1), speaks as 'I, Paul' (1:23), and ends with a greeting in Paul's own hand (4:18). Its greetings and couriers match Philemon, which is broadly accepted as Paul's.

Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Origen and Eusebius took the letter as Paul's. The New Jerome Biblical Commentary (1990), as quoted in the Wikipedia survey of the letter, says the earliest outside evidence is from the middle to late 100s (Marcion's canon, Irenaeus, the Muratorian canon) and that the traditional view stood until 1838. J. B. Lightfoot (1875) defended the letter as one whole against Holtzmann's theory of a later reworking. Among modern defenders the same commentary names Martin, Caird, Houlden, Cannon and Moule.

E. T. Mayerhoff denied Paul's authorship in 1838, calling the letter full of non-Pauline ideas and dependent on Ephesians. The arguments since: vocabulary (Helmut Koester counted 48 words not found elsewhere in Paul, 33 of them found nowhere else in the New Testament); a liturgical, hymn-like style found nowhere else in Paul to the same extent (Werner Kümmel); and teaching with no clear parallel in the undisputed letters: Christ as head of the church his body, victory over the powers, and believers already 'raised with Christ' (2:12; 3:1), where Romans 6:5 puts the resurrection in the future.

Those who hold that Paul wrote it answer that differences can come from growth in Paul's thought, a different occasion, or a different secretary. They note that Galatians, of similar length, has 35 words found nowhere else in the New Testament, so Colossians' count is not unusual. Norman Perrin, who himself thinks the letter is pseudonymous, granted that 'the letter does employ a great deal of traditional material', which can explain the un-Pauline language. Kümmel listed turns of style found in the New Testament only in Paul (for example the 'too' after 'This is why' in 1:9). And the letter's people and plans fit Philemon closely (4:7-17).

A middle view holds that Timothy or another coworker wrote the letter with Paul's approval while Paul was in prison, and Paul signed it (4:18). Eduard Schweizer proposed that Paul and Timothy wrote it together, and James Dunn's commentary is cited for the possibility that Timothy was the secretary. This would explain both the Pauline setting and the different style.

Others see the letter as deutero-Pauline, written after Paul's lifetime by someone who knew his teaching: about AD 70 (Gnilka) or about AD 80 (Lohse, who regards it as the product of a Pauline school, probably at Ephesus). Those who hold this view see writing in a revered teacher's name as a practice of the time; others doubt that the first readers would have accepted it had they known.

The New Jerome Biblical Commentary (1990) says the many differences have 'persuaded most modern scholars that Paul did not write Colossians', and takes that position itself; on that account the later-follower view is the majority among critical scholars. A substantial minority defends Paul's authorship, with or without a secretary, and the traditional view of the churches is that Paul wrote it. This site could not check a more recent count of scholars. The letter's teaching is the same whichever view is taken; the Plain English Translation follows the text as written ('Paul').

audience.to: The believers at Colossae, a small town in the Lycus valley of Phrygia, in the Roman province of Asia, about 12 miles (19 km) east of Laodicea and near Hierapolis. They were mostly Gentiles (1:21, 27; 2:13, 'the uncircumcision of your flesh'), converted by Epaphras, a Colossian (1:7; 4:12), probably during Paul's years at Ephesus (Acts 19:10). Paul had never visited them (2:1). They met in houses, among them Philemon's (Philemon 2), and their households included slaves such as Onesimus (4:9). Jews lived in the region. A later church council at Laodicea forbade Christians to 'invoke angels', and Theodoret wrote in the 400s that the practice Paul denounces 'long remained in Phrygia and Pisidia' (both quoted by Lightfoot).
audience.why: News from Epaphras showed that the church was being pressed by a teaching the letter calls 'philosophy' and 'human tradition' (2:8): its teachers judged believers over food, festivals, new moons and Sabbaths (2:16), praised fasting and 'the worship of angels', claimed visions (2:18), and laid down rules ('Do not taste! Do not even touch!', 2:21). The letter answers that the readers already have all the fullness of God in Christ (2:9-10), that the powers they feared were created in him and defeated at the cross (1:16; 2:15), and that holiness is shown not by rules and visions but by a new life of love in ordinary households (3:1-4:1). Knowing the readers changes the reading: the high claims about Christ are not abstract theology but pastoral care for Gentile believers who were being told that they were incomplete.
views: Paul to a church he had not met
Paul, in prison, writes through Tychicus to a church founded by his coworker, at the same time as he writes to Philemon, one of its members.
A Pauline writer to a later generation
A follower of Paul writes after his death to the churches of the Lycus valley, using Paul's voice to address a later form of the same threat.

outline: Thanks for the good news among them; Epaphras
Prayer for knowledge, strength and thanks; rescued into the Son's kingdom
The hymn: Christ the image of God, firstborn of creation and of the dead
Paul's sufferings and his task: the mystery, Christ in you
Walk in him: the fullness of deity, circumcision, baptism, the cross and the powers
Shadow and body: food, days, angels, rules
Take off the old self, put on the new: love, peace, the word, song
Tychicus and Onesimus, greetings, the letter from Laodicea, Paul's signature

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Colossians against the Lycus valley: a declining Phrygian town beside rich Laodicea and Hierapolis, Jewish communities, Phrygian religion, earthquakes, Roman households with their slaves, and Paul in prison. Used by J. B. Lightfoot and Clinton Arnold.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the letter was made: whether Paul, a coworker such as Timothy, or a later follower wrote it; how it relates to Ephesians and Philemon; whether 1:15-20 is an earlier hymn; what the 'philosophy' was; and what the manuscripts read.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Follows the letter's design: thanksgiving and prayer flowing into the hymn, the wordplays (fullness and filled, the umpire, stripping off), the vice and virtue lists, the clothing images, and the household code's pairs.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads the letter's Jewish world: Wisdom language for Christ (Proverbs 8), circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6), the Sabbath, new moons and festivals, Jewish mysticism and the angels' worship, Israel's titles given to Gentiles, and how Jewish readers hear 2:16-17.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: How the churches have read it: the Arian controversy over 'firstborn' and the Nicene answer, the fathers on 1:24, 2:15 and 2:18, Calvin and the Catholic tradition on 1:24, baptism and circumcision in Reformed, Lutheran, Orthodox and Baptist teaching, the Sabbath in Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, Baptist and Adventist teaching, and the honor of angels.

sections.b:
Colossians is short enough to read aloud in twenty minutes, as its first hearers did (4:16). Its argument has a simple shape. Chapter 1 says who Christ is (1:15-20) and what he has done for the readers (1:21-23). Chapter 2 draws the conclusion: since all the fullness of God is in Christ, and you are full in him, do not let anyone sell you anything more (2:8-23). Chapters 3 and 4 say what life in him looks like: not visions and rules, but a new way of treating one another at home, at church and in town.

The key words are kept the same in the Plain English Translation: fullness (1:19; 2:9-10), all things (1:16-20), mystery (1:26-27; 2:2; 4:3), the basic elements of the world (2:8, 20), rulers and authorities (1:16; 2:10, 15), head and body (1:18; 2:19), walk (1:10; 2:6; 3:7; 4:5), and thanks (1:3, 12; 2:7; 3:15-17; 4:2).

Much of Colossians has close parallels in Ephesians: redemption and forgiveness (1:14; Ephesians 1:7), reconciliation through the cross (1:20-22; Ephesians 2:13-16), the head and the body (2:19; Ephesians 4:16), the old and new self (3:9-10; Ephesians 4:22-24), the vice lists (3:5-8; Ephesians 4:31; 5:3-6), psalms, hymns and songs (3:16; Ephesians 5:19), the household code (3:18-4:1; Ephesians 5:22-6:9), buying up the moment (4:5; Ephesians 5:16), and Tychicus (4:7-8; Ephesians 6:21-22, nearly word for word). This site's Plain English Translation uses the same English where the Greek is the same and different English where it differs, so readers can compare.

Many scholars think Colossians is the earlier letter and that Ephesians draws on it, either because Paul wrote both at nearly the same time, or because a later writer used Colossians as a model. E. T. Mayerhoff argued the reverse in 1838, that Colossians depends on Ephesians.

Philemon is a private letter to a believer at Colossae about his slave Onesimus. Colossians names Onesimus as 'one of you' (4:9), and both letters send greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke, and mention Archippus. Most scholars think the two went together with Tychicus and Onesimus. Read together, they show the household code of 3:22-4:1 in a real case: a master told to give his slaves 'what is just and what is equal' (4:1), and asked by Paul to take his slave back as a beloved brother (Philemon 16).

The Plain English Translation follows the SBL Greek New Testament, checked against NA28 and the Tyndale House edition. It departs from the SBL edition once: at 1:21-22 it follows NA28 and Tyndale House ('he has reconciled you') against SBL's 'you were reconciled', the reading of P46 and Vaticanus. It departs from NA28 three times, each time with SBL: 'our' at 1:7 (NA28 'your'), 'eating or drinking' at 2:16 (NA28 'and'), and 'a slave of Christ' at 4:12 (NA28 adds 'Jesus' in brackets). At 4:15 it follows SBL and NA28 ('her house') against Tyndale House ('their house'). The main variants: the greeting (1:2), 'our' or 'your' (1:7, where the editions disagree), 'through his blood' added from Ephesians (1:14), the tangled phrase 'the mystery of God, Christ' (2:2), 'what he has seen' or 'has not seen' (2:18), and Nympha's house (4:15). The oldest manuscript of Colossians is P46, a papyrus codex of Paul's letters from about AD 200.

spec.title: Claude's theory: one letter for two audiences in one house
spec.body: Colossians and Philemon arrived together, carried by Tychicus and Onesimus (4:7-9). Colossians was read aloud to the whole church (4:16), and that church met in Philemon's house (Philemon 2). I suggest that the household code was heard by Philemon and Onesimus in the same room, and that its weight on slaves (four verses, against one to masters) and its pointed word to masters (4:1, 'what is just and what is equal ... you too have a Lord in heaven') were written with that scene in mind. The public letter set the frame (slaves serve the Lord, masters answer to him, and 'there is no favoritism') and the private letter asked Philemon to go further. This overlaps with the common view that the two letters were sent together, but goes beyond it in reading 3:22-4:1 as shaped for Philemon's household. If Colossians was written later, the theory falls.

prompts: A small house church in a Phrygian hill town at night: a dozen men, women and children and two slaves sit on mats in a courtyard while a reader holds up a papyrus letter. Above them, drawn like a cave painting across the night sky, a great figure of light from whom stars, mountains, birds, crowned angels and tiny people all spread out like branches from a trunk. Sketched by hand onto old parchment mixed with ochre cave-drawing marks and soft modern watercolor; wobbling ink lines, torn edges; no hard rectangular frame.
The IOU nailed to the cross

A rough wooden cross drawn in charcoal, with a crumpled handwritten papyrus bill of debt pinned to it by a single nail; the ink letters are running and fading as if washed away. Below, a broken line of small figures in chains, once proud spirits wearing crowns, walk behind in a Roman victory parade. Ancient manuscript style mixed with cave-painting figures and modern ink wash, on a scroll with soft torn edges.
Three towns in the Lycus valley

A hand-drawn map on a scroll: the Lycus river winding through a green valley, the white terraces of Hierapolis glittering on one side, rich Laodicea with columns and a theater, and small Colossae on its mound under a mountain. Tiny figures walk the road between them carrying letters: one with a satchel (Tychicus), one young man beside him (Onesimus). Sketchy ink lines, ochre and sepia washes, no hard border.
reading: J. B. Lightfoot, Saint Paul's Epistles to the Colossians and to Philemon (1875)
The classic commentary on the Greek, with long essays on Colossae, the 'Colossian heresy' and the Essenes, and on the letter from Laodicea. Free online at Project Gutenberg.
James D. G. Dunn, The Epistles to the Colossians and to Philemon: A Commentary on the Greek Text (New International Greek Testament Commentary, 1996)
A commentary on the Greek text of both letters.
N. T. Wright, Colossians and Philemon (Tyndale New Testament Commentaries, 1986)
A short commentary on both letters.
Clinton E. Arnold, The Colossian Syncretism (1995)
A study of the 'philosophy' against the background of Phrygian folk religion, magic and angel veneration.
